papers.title_in_file: HARNESSING CYC TO ANSWER CLINICAL RESEARCHERS’ AD HOC QUERIES
papers.version_note: AI Magazine, Volume 31, Number 3, Fall 2010 (per the text header).
papers.what_it_is: A system paper describing SRA, a Cyc-based interactive system built with Cleveland Clinic for composing and answering clinical researchers' ad hoc queries, with deployment figures and design details.

assertions.value: The authors state that by extending Cyc's ontology and KB approximately 2%, Cycorp and Cleveland Clinic Foundation built a system, SRA, to answer clinical researchers' ad hoc queries.
quotes: By extending Cyc’s ontology and KB approximately 2%, Cycorp and Cleveland Clinic Foundation (CCF) have built a system to answer clinical researchers’ ad hoc queries.
assertions.certainty_reason: Vendor authors describe their own system; no measurement of the 2% figure is given in the body.

assertions.value: The authors report that before SRA about 300 new queries per year were posed and answered in the cardiothoracic surgery, cardiac catheterization and percutaneous coronary intervention domains, most needing 1-10 weeks; in 2010, using SRA, such queries take 5-50 minutes (occasionally several hours) and over 2,000 queries are processed each week.
quotes: Prior to SRA, approximately 300 new queries in those domains had been posed and answered each year, with most queries requiring 1-10 weeks (occasionally several tens of weeks) of real time
in 2010, using SRA, such
queries take 5-50 minutes to produce satisfactory answers (occasionally several hours), and over 2,000 queries are processed each week.
assertions.certainty_reason: Authors report deployment figures for their own system; no method for the timing is given.
assertions.reader_inference: The 2,000 per week figure includes persistent bundles re-run on a schedule, as the paper says, so it is not a count of new ad hoc queries.

assertions.value: The authors report that persistent query bundles are re-run each month for internal quality testing and quarterly for external reporting: one bundle of 275 queries produces the data CCF needs to report to STS and a bundle of 256 queries produces the data for ACC.
quotes: persistent bundles of queries in those domains are re-run each month (for internal quality testing purposes) and quarterly (for external third-party reporting purposes)
one bundle of 275 queries produces the procedures and outcomes data CCF needs to report to STS
a bundle of 256 queries produces the data CCF needs to report to ACC (the American College of Cardiology).
assertions.certainty_reason: Authors describe their own deployment.

assertions.value: The authors report that email logs tracking 900 queries over the last few years at CCF show a mean completion time of approximately one month of real time through a two-intermediary process, effectively limiting researchers to about a dozen such queries per year.
quotes: the email logs tracking 900 of these queries over the last few years at CCF show a mean time for this process to complete of approximately one month of real time, effectively limiting researchers to about a dozen such queries per year.
assertions.certainty_reason: One site's email-log measurement reported by the authors; the method is not detailed.

assertions.value: The authors state their aim for SRA is to let physicians pose complex ad hoc questions directly and have them understood and answered in four minutes rather than four weeks.
quotes: Our aim with SRA is to enable physicians to pose their complex ad hoc questions directly, getting them understood and answered in four minutes rather than four weeks.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states its own design aim in Section 2.

assertions.value: The authors list five AI challenges between the enquirer and an answer: understanding the literal query, understanding the intended query, finding the answer from heterogeneous sources, presenting answers usefully, and failing soft with semantic search.
quotes: Challenge 1: Getting the literal query understood
Challenge 2: Getting the intended query understood.
Challenge 3: Given a complete, unambiguous, logical form of the intended query, finding the answer to that query.
Challenge 4: Present the answers to the physician in a useful fashion.
Challenge 5: In cases where the system would otherwise fail to return an answer, it should “fail soft”
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper defines its own five challenges in Section 2.

assertions.value: The authors state that the state of the art of natural language parsing cannot reliably parse even short ad hoc queries such as Q1 into a precise, unambiguous logical or database query representation.
quotes: But the state of the art of natural language parsing today cannot reliably parse even shorter ad hoc queries such as Q1 into a precise, unambiguous logical or data base query language representation.
assertions.certainty_reason: An author claim about the state of the art in 2010, with no supporting evaluation.

assertions.value: The authors state that SPARQL optimization had not yet become available for RDF/OWL triple stores, resulting in queries taking orders of magnitude too long, and that they expect the problem to solve itself in the next five years.
quotes: for which such optimization has not yet become available, resulting in queries taking orders of magnitude too long.
We expect this problem to solve itself in the next five years, as commercial SPARQL optimization catches up with SQL optimization.
assertions.certainty_reason: An author claim and forecast with no measurement.

assertions.value: The authors state that because accurate parsing of complex medical queries to precise logical representations is beyond the state of the art, SRA's main process is an interactive clarification dialogue; the user selects query fragments, shown as English fill-in-the-blank paraphrases, and tells the system to combine them.
quotes: Since accurate parsing of complex medical queries to precise logical representations is well beyond the state of the art, the main process used is an interactive clarification dialogue between the system and the user
The user highlights the fragments representing parts of the query they had in mind, and tells the system to combine them.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper describes its own workflow in Section 3.1.

assertions.value: The authors state that SRA combines fragments into a single predicate calculus query using the full Cyc KB and inference engine, and that two of the most important decisions are which variables unify and the type and scope of each quantifier.
quotes: SRA brings the entire Cyc knowledge base and inference engine to bear in support of the combination process.
(a) which variables unify with which other variables (i.e., refer to the same thing)? and (b) what is the type of each quantifier (universal or existential) and the scope/nesting of the quantifiers?
assertions.certainty_reason: Stated description of the system's design.

assertions.value: The authors state that constructing hard-wired combination rules for the whole vocabulary would be impractical, and in a footnote that the cardinality of such a set would exceed the number of atoms in the universe.
quotes: it would be impractical5 to construct the corresponding set of hard-wired combination rules.
The cardinality of such a set would exceed the number of atoms in the universe.
assertions.certainty_reason: An author claim given without derivation.

assertions.value: The authors state that by leveraging the existing Cyc KB, only project specifics needed adding, for example that AVRs are surgical procedures and that pericardial aortic valves are medical implants, and that Cyc has understood the disjointness of event and tangible object collections since 1985.
quotes: it was only necessary to add the specifics for this project: for example, that AVRs are surgical procedures, and that pericardial aortic valves are medical implants6.
Cyc has, since 1985, understood the sort of disjointness between those collections (Lenat and Guha 1989)
assertions.certainty_reason: An author claim about reuse without a stated count of assertions added.

assertions.value: The authors report that for the simple query shown in the interface, 1132 answers were found.
quotes: For the simple query shown, 1132 answers were found.
assertions.certainty_reason: A single illustrative query result.

assertions.value: The authors report that the queried data store represented a device as a Model9000IDE rather than a pericardial aortic valve, and that Cyc background knowledge supplied that each 9000IDE is a pericardial aortic valve prosthesis, so that an answer could be justified in natural language.
quotes: The data store being queried did not represent this device as a pericardial aortic valve, but as a Model9000IDE; Cyc provides the background knowledge that each 9000IDE is a pericardial aortic valve prosthesis
assertions.certainty_reason: A single worked example shown by the authors.

assertions.value: The authors report that the Cyc KB holds one rule that adult males have left atrial enlargement if left atrial diameter exceeds 4.2cm, and another that for adult females the cutoff is 3.8cm.
quotes: the Cyc KB has
one rule that says that adult males fall into that category if their left atrial diameter
exceeds 4.2cm, and another rule that says that for adult females the cutoff is 3.8cm.)
assertions.certainty_reason: A domain rule the authors report as encoded, shown as an example; not independently sourced in the paper.

assertions.value: The authors state that users have a difficult time keeping temporal constraints straight when presented as English phrases and that doing so is much easier when they are also drawn graphically in a Time Graph.
quotes: It turns out that users have a difficult time keeping temporal constraints straight, if they are presented as English phrases; doing so is much easier when they are also drawn graphically.
assertions.certainty_reason: An author observation with no reported user study.

assertions.value: The authors report that they metered SRA's use of Cyc assertions entered before the collaboration began in 2007 and found that hundreds of pre-existing pieces of prior and tacit knowledge were used for each ad hoc query.
quotes: we metered the SRA system’s use of pre-existing Cyc knowledge (that is, assertions entered into Cyc before our collaboration with CCF started in 2007).
hundreds of preexisting pieces of prior and tacit knowledge in Cyc were used for each ad hoc query.
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one study; no distribution or method detail is given.

assertions.value: The authors state that they avoided the most sophisticated available parsing techniques because they do not produce interpretations consistently and rapidly enough for a predictable user experience, and use a shallower approach based on identifying semantic terms, augmented with a specific parser for relations such as temporal constraints.
quotes: We have therefore avoided the use of the most sophisticated parsing techniques available in the Cyc platform and elsewhere in NLP research
they do not do so consistently enough and rapidly enough for a predictable user experience.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states a design choice and scope of its own system.

assertions.value: The authors report that around 24% of the 126,000 most accessed Wikipedia pages from a typical hour had a corresponding existing Cyc concept, and that term coverage is nearly complete for domains with custom knowledge representation such as cardiothoracic surgery.
quotes: Coverage is already high (around 24% of the 126,000 most accessed Wikipedia pages from a typical hour had a corresponding existing Cyc concept)
term coverage is nearly complete.
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical figure from one sample reported by the authors; the sampling method is not described.
assertions.reader_inference: The paper calls 24% 'high'; that is the authors' judgment, not a comparison against a baseline.

assertions.value: The authors report that the SRA sense filter, a decision tree over Cyc ontology classes, was initially trained by automatically tagging and then manually annotating the relevance of concepts found in 29 example query sentences.
quotes: the SRA filter was initially trained, for example, by automatically tagging and then manually annotating the relevance of the concepts found in a mere 29 example query sentences.
assertions.certainty_reason: A training-set size reported by the authors; no accuracy figure is given.
assertions.reader_inference: No filter accuracy is reported in the paper, so the training-set size alone does not show how well the filter works.

assertions.value: The authors state that SRA's expectation-driving assertions for the medical domain were generated manually by knowledge engineers with domain experts, and that for broader applications such expectations could be generated by forward inference.
quotes: SRA’s expectation-driving assertions for the medical domain have been generated manually by knowledge engineers, in consultation with domain experts, to maximize usability
For broader applications, however, and where less control is needed, such expectations can be generated by forward inference.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states how its own assertions were produced.

assertions.value: The authors state that mixed semantic and syntactic templates are used to recognize temporal constructions, for example matching the pattern for an event between two temporal things yields a temporallyBetween-Inclusive formula.
quotes: mixed semantic/syntactic templates are used to recognize and understand temporal constructions.
causes its arguments to be interpreted as (temporallyBetween-Inclusive <arg1> <arg2> <arg3>).
assertions.certainty_reason: Design of the system's own template, stated in Section 3.2.2.

assertions.value: The authors state that in the typical case shown in the query-composition figure Cyc inference eliminates all possible combinations of a new fragment with the existing query but the correct one in a fraction of a second.
quotes: In this surprisingly typical case, it is able to eliminate all possibilities but the correct one in a fraction of a second.
assertions.certainty_reason: A single illustrated case, with no timing table.

assertions.value: The authors state that if two added clauses have descriptions differing only in specificity, such as a surgery and a valve repair, they are assumed to refer to different entities, although it is logically possible they are the same.
quotes: if two clauses are added with descriptions that differ only with respect to specificity (i.e a description of a surgery, and a valve repair), they are assumed to refer to different entities
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states a heuristic of its own system.

assertions.value: The authors state that for variable and column names, 1750 denotesArgInReln assertions exist in the KB, and otherwise the most specific type constraint that can be rendered as a non-plural noun, has not been used elsewhere, and is not more than 30 characters long is used.
quotes: There are 1750 such assertions in the KB
the first one that can be rendered as a non-plural noun, has not been used elsewhere, and is not more than 30 characters long, is used.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states its own rule in Section 3.2.3.

assertions.value: The authors report that a user search for 'heart attack' returned relevant pages of the Outcomes booklet, which does not contain that term, because Cyc knew it denotes myocardial infarction and that CABG is a common treatment after MI, while avoiding irrelevant pages that a string-based search would include.
quotes: But the Outcomes booklet does not contain that colloquial term anywhere.
relevant “hits” are returned because the Cyc ontology knew that “heart attack” was a denotation for myocardial infarction
allowed it to not retrieve those irrelevant pages even though a string-based search engine would not have understood and would have included those false positives.
assertions.certainty_reason: A single illustrative example; no precision or recall is reported.
assertions.reader_inference: No retrieval accuracy is measured against a keyword baseline, so the claim of fewer false positives rests on one example.

assertions.value: The authors state that fail-soft capabilities were implemented in CAE and applied experimentally to outcome data in end-user search, but have not been integrated deeply into SRA's initial research cohort selection application.
quotes: they have not been integrated deeply into the SRA’s initial research cohort selection application.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states the limit of its own system in footnote 4.

assertions.value: The authors report that adding the cardiac catheterization domain involves approximately 500 new concepts and 6500 new assertions, about half of them lexical, tying concepts to standards including Snomed and ICD-9 and -10, and that the other half involve one or more of the preexisting 500,000 concepts in the Cyc ontology.
quotes: The approximately 500 new concepts and 6500 new assertions which are currently being added, for this domain,
About half of the 6500 new assertions for this domain are lexical assertions
preexisting 500,000 concepts in the Cyc ontology
tying it to standards including Snomed and ICD-9 and -10
assertions.certainty_reason: A count the authors report for work in progress, not a completed measurement.

assertions.value: The authors state that initial acquisition of concepts, terminological assertions and medical knowledge assertions for each domain is done top-down, using a reference text for cardiac catheterization a published handbook first, then expanding from a sample of clinical research and clinical queries.
quotes: The initial acquisition of concepts, terminological assertions, and medical knowledge assertions for each domain is done top-down.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states its own acquisition method.

assertions.value: The authors report being surprised to find empirically that condensing, formatting and exporting answers has been one of the biggest factors affecting whether and to what extent physicians directly use SRA.
quotes: So we were surprised to find that empirically this has been one of the biggest factors affecting whether and to what extent physicians directly use the SRA.
assertions.certainty_reason: An author observation of use; no usage data is given.

assertions.value: The authors state that, at least in the medical domains explored to date, natural language understanding of detailed queries can be performed largely compositionally, building and refining pieces of the query rather than reasoning about the query as a whole.
quotes: natural language understanding for detailed queries, even quite long queries, can – at least in the medical domains explored to date – be performed in a largely compositional fashion
assertions.certainty_reason: An author observation limited to the domains explored.

assertions.value: The authors state as future work: data-driven clinical practice that retrieves treatment options and outcomes for a patient, explicit user and task models, a smarter data entry capability, and weak and strong forms of Cyc-based semantic searching; for the weak form they say success depends on the algorithms developed.
quotes: Clinical Use: Although the SRA has been developed in the context of cohort-selection for clinical outcome studies
Unlike the other SRA extensions we have just described, this one may succeed or fail based more on the algorithms developed for it.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper presents these as not yet done.

assertions.value: The authors state they do not yet have preliminary results on the extent and way clinical researchers and clinicians will use the semantic search capability, and will discover this empirically.
quotes: One of the factors we do not yet have much in the way of preliminary results about, is the extent and way in which the clinical researcher and the clinician will make use of this capability
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states this limit of its evidence.

assertions.value: The authors conclude that they have made progress in getting SRA to answer physicians' ad hoc queries about patient data orders of magnitude faster than what had been best practices, and speculate that the general public may become the heaviest users once formal query articulation is fast and easy to use.
quotes: We have made progress in getting SRA to answer physicians’ ad hoc queries about patient data orders of magnitude faster than what had been “best practices”
the general public may become the heaviest users
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors' conclusion; no controlled comparison is reported.
assertions.reader_inference: The speed comparison is between the earlier manual process (about one month mean) and SRA (5-50 minutes), both author-reported.

assertions.value: The paper reports deployment figures, worked examples and design descriptions; it reports no controlled evaluation of answer correctness, such as precision or recall of the query understanding, against a reference set.
quotes: Preliminary results are encouraging: SRA is now used to ask each clinical research query involving cardiothoracic surgery
assertions.certainty_reason: A reader observation; the quote only shows the paper's own framing of its results as preliminary.
assertions.reader_inference: This is the reader's observation after reading every section; the paper does not itself say it lacks an accuracy evaluation.
